EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Allen County received damaging ice accumulation of 0.50-0.65 inches. This ice accumulation caused tree and power line damage, which resulted in thousands without power. Snow and sleet accumulation of around 3 inches also impacted the county.

A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Ice amounts ranged from three-tenths to half an inch in northeast Kentucky. In addition to ice, two to three inches of snow fell across the area. Ice accumulations led to power outages and downed some trees near the communities of Flatwoods, Raceland, and Yatesville.

A line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept through northeast Kentucky during the predawn hours of March 16th in response to a passing cold front. Downed trees and power lines were observed in Boyd and Lawrence Counties as a result of these stronger storms. Outside of thunderstorms, a period of strong synoptic winds accompanying this disturbance took place. Surface winds picked up in intensity in the wake of the storms and remained elevated into the morning hours of the 16th. The strongest observation of these winds in northeast Kentucky were noted shortly after the round of storms swept through between 4 and 4:30 AM, where Mesonet stations and the AWOS in Ashland recorded winds ranging from 35 to 42 miles per hour. As high pressure built in from the west on the 16th, gradient winds diminished.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and power line were blown down along Harley Drive south of Louisa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: As the tornado continued following Rough River Lake, it uprooted trees, snapped trees, and blew a metal roof off a house before crossing back into Grayson County.

Ahead of an approaching cold front, unseasonably warm air surged into the region on a potent low-level jet, with temperatures reaching record levels at London and Jackson. Widespread non-convective wind gusts between 30 and 50 mph occurred during the afternoon.||As the cold front moved in during the evening, a pre-frontal squall line (QLCS) developed in a high shear environment and tracked across the Commonwealth. The most intense measured wind gust was 70 mph at the London-Corbin Airport ASOS. Elsewhere, the storms resulted in structural damage, scattered downed trees, and a few power outages before a sharp cold front crossed the area, ushering in a much drier and colder airmass.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An amateur radio operator reported that a metal carport had been flipped and mangled in the Keavy area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado uprooted trees as it moved along Rough River Lake.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A robust cold front crossed eastern Kentucky late in the night of March 22nd and early on the morning of the 23rd. The system was characterized by a sharp transition between a warm antecedent air mass and a significantly cooler, drier post-frontal air mass. The primary impact was driven by a southeastward-diving, outflow-reinforced frontal boundary that preceded the main area of showers. While convective activity was relatively weak, this hybrid outflow/frontal boundary produced localized high wind gusts in Fleming County, downing multiple large trees, one of which resulted in structural damage to a residence.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media report indicated that multiple large trees were blown down by intense winds. Specifically, two large trees came down on a property along Dillon Lane and one of them hit a house. There was no precipitation observed with the wind.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An emergency manager reported a tree blown down near the intersection of Woodland Hl and KY-90.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system pressing through the Great Lakes region on March 13th resulted in a windy day across northeast Kentucky. This was due to the combination of a tightened pressure gradient and strengthening low level jet aloft. Daytime heating helped to create turbulent mixing of these stronger winds down to the surface, especially during the afternoon and early evening hours. Wind gusts in excess of 40 to 50 miles per hour noted in northeast Kentucky resulted in downed trees and power lines across the area. The wind gradually declined after sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Leslie County dispatch reported a tree blown down in the MM 3 to 4 stretch of KY-699 in the vicinity of Smilax.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours on March 11th. Ahead of the front, modest amounts of instability were present, with surface dewpoint temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s, allowing for between 500 and 1000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. With strong flow aloft, deep-layer shear was supportive of strong to severe storms, with shear values around 50-60 knots ahead of the front. Ultimately, ample cloudiness and stronger storms firing over the deep south limited the severe potential over much of Kentucky. However, a couple strong cells were able to make it into southeastern Kentucky, producing scattered instances of wind damage in the Lake Cumberland area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down and the roof was blown off of a trailer along Wisdom Dock Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept through northeast Kentucky during the predawn hours of March 16th in response to a passing cold front. Downed trees and power lines were observed in Boyd and Lawrence Counties as a result of these stronger storms. Outside of thunderstorms, a period of strong synoptic winds accompanying this disturbance took place. Surface winds picked up in intensity in the wake of the storms and remained elevated into the morning hours of the 16th. The strongest observation of these winds in northeast Kentucky were noted shortly after the round of storms swept through between 4 and 4:30 AM, where Mesonet stations and the AWOS in Ashland recorded winds ranging from 35 to 42 miles per hour. As high pressure built in from the west on the 16th, gradient winds diminished.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 7th record-setting early March warmth in the upper 70s and low 80s primed eastern Kentucky for isolated severe weather ahead of an advancing cold front. Strong wind shear and sufficient instability supported a convective line that tracked northwest to southeast across the region during the late afternoon and evening. The primary hazard was damaging straight-line winds, which caused localized utility damage and a power outage in the Jackson area. A sharp temperature drop followed the front, ending the anomalous warmth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media user reported a tree blown down onto a road about 1 mile west northwest of the Bethany community.

A prolonged period of wintry weather impacted eastern Kentucky from February 22 into February 24, 2026, as a deep upper-level trough over the eastern United States funneled a moist, modified polar airmass into the region. This setup established a persistent northwesterly upslope flow regime, resulting in scattered to numerous snow showers. These showers were frequently cellular in nature and produced squall-like conditions at some locations.||Accumulations varied significantly across the region due to the convective and orographic nature of the event. While many locations near and west of Pottsville Escarpment saw only a dusting to an inch, higher terrain in the southeast experienced much more substantial totals. The heaviest totals were generally concentrated near the Pine and Black Mountains in the far east, where persistent upslope forcing maximized snowfall. However, isolated similarly heavy swaths were also noted upstream of these higher mountains over portions of Lee and Owsley counties, where convective snow bands persisted for extended periods. Despite high snow-to-liquid ratios of 15:1 to 40:1 for most locations, leading to dry, fluffy snow, the intensity of the showers caused slick and hazardous travel conditions on untreated roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An isolated, heavy swath of snow developed upstream of the main eastern Kentucky mountain ranges. A trained spotter and retired NWS employee at Belle Point measured a storm total of 6.5 inches of snow by 0930EST on the 23rd. A CO-OP observer 4 miles north of Beattyville recorded 2.6 inches during the same event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A complex mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain impacted Breathitt County. An initial 1.2 inches of snow was reported at WFO Jackson by midnight of January 25th. A half inch of sleet then feel between midnight and 220EST. Freezing rain then fell for much of the day on the 25th, leaving a flat ice accretion total of 0.45 inches measured at 1909EST. Additional light snow occurred on the back of the system. The combined weight downed a large tree across KY Highway 205 near Paxton at 1100EST on the 25th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level trough and an intensifying coastal low off the Eastern Seaboard combined to produce a fluffy snowfall event across southeastern Kentucky from January 30th through January 31st, 2026. As the coastal system intensified into a powerful Nor'easter, the band pivoted and became nearly stationary along the Kentucky-Virginia border, leading to an extended period of light to moderate snowfall.||The highest accumulations were concentrated in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Harlan counties, where totals reached 4.0 to 5.0 inches. Because of the extremely cold Arctic airmass in place, snow-to-liquid ratios were high, ranging from 14:1 to 19:1, resulting in a very dry, powdery snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Impactful snowfall reached warning criteria across portions of Pike County. At 0855EST on the 31st, the State Police Post in Coal Run estimated 4.0 inches of snow.
